textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio de divulgacao, no registro das colunas de opiniao usadas pela banca
textos.conteudo:
Every few months a sentence appears online with a famous name attached to it: Mark Twain, Einstein, Maya Angelou. The sentence is usually neat, quotable [fácil de citar] and slightly too polished [polido] to be true. Researchers who track these attributions [atribuições] have noticed a pattern. The names that attract false quotations are almost never obscure ones. They belong to writers and scientists the public already trusts, and the sentences assigned to them tend to express ideas the public already holds.

This suggests that misattribution is not simply a failure of memory. A forgotten source is replaced by a famous one because the famous name does work that the sentence alone cannot do: it converts an opinion into an authority. When a librarian traced [rastreou] one widely shared Twain quotation to a magazine article published fourteen years after his death, the correction circulated for a week and the false version returned.

What is striking is how rarely anyone benefits from the deception [engano]. There is no industry of quotation forgery [falsificação], no profit in it. The sentences spread because each person who repeats one is paying a small compliment to a writer they admire, and because verifying it would take four minutes that nobody has. One historian of reading calls this 'affectionate error' — a mistake made out of regard rather than malice [má-fé].

She argues that the phenomenon tells us less about our relationship with facts than about our relationship with reputation. We do not so much believe that Twain said the sentence. We believe that he would have.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem analitica de revista economica internacional
textos.conteudo:
For two decades, several governments in Africa and South Asia held their currencies at official rates that no private trader would accept. Importers who could obtain dollars at the official price made fortunes; everyone else bought them on a parallel market [mercado paralelo] at two or three times that rate. The gap was not a secret. It was, in effect, a subsidy [subsídio] paid to whoever had access to the central bank, and its beneficiaries were rarely the poor.

When such a country finally lets its currency float [flutuar], the immediate result is a shock. Imported fuel, medicine and wheat cost more in local money on the first morning, and the increase is visible to everyone. What is not visible is the earlier transfer of wealth to the well connected, because it happened at a counter [balcão], in silence, over years. A finance minister who devalues [desvaloriza] is therefore blamed for a price rise that was already being paid — only, until then, by people without the standing [posição] to complain. This is the arithmetic that turns an adjustment [ajuste] economists call overdue [atrasado] into a political emergency.

Lenders have learned to attach conditions to the loans that accompany such reforms: fuel subsidies are to be removed, arrears [atrasados] to suppliers cleared, the central bank made formally independent. The record of these programmes is mixed. Where governments paired devaluation with cash transfers to households, the reforms have survived; where they did not, the streets have often reversed them within a year. The variable that seems to matter is not the size of the correction but whether the population can be shown something in exchange for it.

None of this settles the question of timing. Devaluing during a failed harvest [safra] or an election year has undone governments that would otherwise have been re-elected, and the temptation to postpone [adiar] is strong precisely because the cost of postponement falls on people who are not in the room.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de divulgacao cientifica, no registro das revistas de historia natural usadas pela banca
textos.conteudo:
Biologists studying animals in and around cities have begun to describe them less by where they live than by when. A fox in a European capital is not occupying territory that a rural fox would refuse; it is occupying the same territory at a different hour. Camera traps [armadilhas fotográficas] set in a dozen countries show the same displacement: as human traffic in a green space rises, mammals that were active in daylight shift most of their movement into the four hours after midnight.

The adjustment is fast. In one park, the closure of a footpath [trilha] for repairs was followed within eleven days by deer [cervos] feeding in the middle of the afternoon; when the path reopened, the daylight feeding stopped almost as quickly. The animals do not appear to be learning that people are dangerous. They are reading a timetable [horário], and they revise it as the timetable changes.

The consequence is easy to underestimate. An animal pushed into the night is not merely inconvenienced [incomodado]. It hunts with senses tuned for another light, competes with species that were already nocturnal and, in the case of several herbivores, spends less total time feeding, because the safe window is shorter than the day it replaced. A population can look stable in a census [censo] while every individual in it is eating less.

This is why researchers increasingly argue that conservation inside cities is a question of scheduling rather than of area. Closing a reserve two nights a week may do more for the animals in it than enlarging [ampliar] it — and it costs nothing that a city government would have to buy.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo de revista de relacoes internacionais
textos.conteudo:
The most durable authoritarian governments of the past twenty years have rarely needed to ban an opposition party. They have preferred to register it, audit [auditar] it and fine [multar] it. A civic association is required to declare its foreign funding [financiamento]; the declaration is filed late; the fine exceeds the association's annual budget; the association closes. Nothing in that sequence looks like repression [repressão] from outside, and every step of it can be defended in a courtroom.

The advantage of the method is not efficiency. Prosecuting a treasurer [tesoureiro] over paperwork is slower and more expensive than arresting an organiser. The advantage is that it produces no martyr [mártir] and no photograph. A government that jails a journalist acquires an international problem; a government that bankrupts [leva à falência] the journalist's employer over a licensing dispute acquires a quiet newsroom and a defensible position at the next summit [cúpula].

This is also what makes the method hard to answer. Foreign ministries willing to protest a mass arrest have no vocabulary for a tax audit, and the sanctions [sanções] they have built assume an event — a coup, a stolen election, a killing — rather than a process that takes four years and leaves the constitution untouched. Human rights organisations have begun to count closures of associations rather than arrests, on the argument that the second number no longer measures anything.

Whether the technique is stable is a separate question. Its weakness is that it depends on courts that are compliant [complacentes] but still functioning, and on officials willing to enforce rules they know to be pretexts [pretextos]. Both have proved harder to sustain than the governments using them expected.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem economica de jornal diario
textos.conteudo:
When the price of cocoa [cacau] tripled in eighteen months, the first people to notice were not shoppers. Chocolate on a supermarket shelf in London or São Paulo had been bought under contracts signed a year earlier, and the bar a customer picked up in March reflected a harvest [safra] and a price from the previous season. The delay is a feature of the trade, not an accident: manufacturers buy forward [compram a termo] precisely so that a bad year in West Africa does not arrive in their factories all at once.

What the delay conceals [esconde] is where the loss lands. In several producing countries the farm-gate price [preço na porteira] is fixed by a state board before the season begins, which protects growers when the world price collapses and excludes them from it when the world price triples. Farmers watching a record market from inside a fixed contract have few options, and the one most of them take — cutting spending on fertiliser [fertilizante] and on replacing ageing trees — guarantees a weaker harvest in the years that follow. A price spike [pico de preço] can therefore reduce future supply rather than call it forth.

Manufacturers, meanwhile, respond in ways the label does not announce. The bar shrinks [encolhe] by five grams, the cocoa share falls by two percentage points, a filling [recheio] grows. Surveys suggest that shoppers register the price on the shelf far more reliably than either change.

By the time the shelf price finally moves, the market that caused it may have turned. That mismatch [descompasso] is one reason commodity shocks are so often described, afterwards, as having been obvious — and so rarely acted on while they are happening.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio breve de suplemento cultural
textos.conteudo:
There is a particular kind of shame attached to an unread book. It sits on the shelf, its spine uncracked [lombada intacta], and every time its owner walks past, the purchase is quietly repeated as a failure. Bookshops encourage the feeling, and so does every list of titles one is supposed to have finished by a certain age.

The writer Umberto Eco kept a library of some thirty thousand volumes, of which he had read a small fraction. Visitors reacted in one of two ways. Most treated the collection as a trophy and asked how many he had got through. A few understood that the unread portion was the point. A library, Eco argued, is not a record of what its owner knows. It is an instrument, and its value lies in what it holds that the owner does not yet know and may one day need.

Framed that way, the shame inverts [inverte-se]. A shelf of books you have finished is a closed archive of a past self. A shelf of books you have not finished is a map of the questions you have decided are worth keeping within reach. The first tells you where you have been; only the second is of any use when you arrive somewhere unfamiliar.

There is a limit, of course. An instrument nobody ever reaches for is furniture [mobília], and a collection assembled to be photographed is not a library at all. But the ordinary case — the book bought in good faith, opened twice, still waiting — deserves better than the guilt [culpa] it usually attracts.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem economica internacional
textos.conteudo:
A coat dropped into a charity bin [caixa de doação] in a European city begins a journey that almost nobody who donates one imagines. It is sorted by hand, graded [classificado], compressed into a bale [fardo] weighing forty-five kilos, sold by weight to an exporter and shipped to a market several thousand kilometres away, where a trader buys the bale without being able to inspect what is inside it.

That last detail carries most of the trade's economics. The trader is buying a lottery ticket. A good bale holds garments [peças de roupa] that will sell within a week at a healthy margin; a bad one is full of items too worn, too heavy for the climate, or printed with a slogan nobody local wants. The share that cannot be sold does not go back to Europe. It is burned, buried or left where the market ends, and its disposal [descarte] is paid for by the town that received it, not by the country that sent it.

Defenders of the trade point out that it clothes millions of people cheaply and supports a long chain of traders, tailors [alfaiates] and repairers who make a living from it. That is true, and it is why proposals to ban imports outright have met resistance from the very workers such bans are meant to protect. Critics reply that the same flow has made it close to impossible to build a domestic clothing industry, since no new garment can compete on price with a used one that arrived as somebody else's surplus [excedente].

Both sides are describing one fact from opposite ends. The bale is cheap because the coat was free, and the coat was free because the person who bought it new replaced it long before it wore out. Whatever is decided at the port, the volume is set in the shop where the coat was bought.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de divulgacao cientifica com enfoque critico
textos.conteudo:
For twenty years, one of the most repeated findings in popular science has been that the trees of a forest are joined underground by fungal threads [filamentos fúngicos] through which they share sugars, send warnings and support their weaker neighbours. The image is irresistible: a forest as a cooperative, with the old feeding the young.

The underlying biology is not in dispute. Fungi do form networks that link the roots [raízes] of different trees, and carbon does move between plants along them. What a group of researchers has questioned is everything built on top of that. Reviewing the field studies most often cited, they found that few had measured transfer in a mature forest rather than in pots; that the quantities moved were small next to what a tree produces for itself; and that in several cases the direction of movement was never established — carbon was detected in a neighbour without any evidence that the first tree had sent it rather than simply lost it.

The critics are careful about what they are claiming. They do not argue that the networks are absent or unimportant. They argue that a hypothesis was promoted to a fact somewhere between the journal and the documentary, and that once a finding acquires a memorable name it becomes very hard to test, because every later study is read either as confirming the story or as missing the point.

The episode is now cited more often as a case study in how science reaches the public than as a question about forests — which its authors find mildly ironic, and which is, they add, an instance of the very problem they were describing.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo de politica internacional
textos.conteudo:
A handful of small states have built a foreign policy out of being the room. They host the talks, keep the archives, run the arbitration [arbitragem] court and, when a prisoner exchange needs an aircraft that neither side will supply, supply the aircraft. None of this rests on military weight, and that is the point: a mediator with an army large enough to matter is a party [parte interessada], not a venue [sede].

The service is more demanding than it looks. It requires a legal system whose rulings both sides expect to be enforced, a banking system able to hold money nobody will admit to owning and — hardest of all — a record of never leaking [vazar]. That record takes decades to build and one afternoon to destroy, which is why states in this business are so conservative about the disputes they agree to take. Turning a mediation down is often the more valuable move.

The returns are real but indirect. Hosting negotiations does not itself pay well. What it buys is a seat at conversations far above the country's size, an insurance policy against being ignored and a professional class — lawyers, translators, insurers — whose expertise attracts business that has nothing to do with diplomacy.

The vulnerability is structural. The role depends on the major powers continuing to want a neutral venue at all, and there have been decades in which they did not. A country that has organised its economy around being trusted by everyone has very little to fall back on in a period when nobody is talking.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre recursos naturais
textos.conteudo:
Sand is the most consumed solid material on earth once water is set aside, and almost none of it can come from a desert. Wind-blown grains are too round and too smooth to lock together in concrete; the grains that work are angular ones, shaped by moving water, and they are found in riverbeds, floodplains [planícies de inundação] and on the seabed. This is why a country can sit in the middle of the largest desert on the planet and still import sand.

The consequences are mostly local and mostly invisible from a city. Taking sand out of a riverbed lowers the water table [lençol freático] that nearby farms depend on, undercuts [solapa] the foundations of bridges and lets salt water travel further up a delta, which quietly changes what can be grown there. None of these effects shows up in the price of a cubic metre of concrete, and each of them arrives years after the extraction that caused it.

Because the material is heavy and cheap, it is rarely worth carrying far, which means the market is not one market but thousands of small ones, each within a short drive of a building site. That structure defeats the usual tools. There is no global exchange to regulate, no small group of exporters to negotiate with, and enforcement falls to whichever local authority sits nearest the river — often the one with the least capacity to stand up to the people doing the digging.

Substitutes exist. Crushed rock, recycled demolition waste and manufactured sand all work, and all cost more than taking material out of a river at night. Until that comparison changes, the substitutes will stay where they are.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio de historia da tecnologia
textos.conteudo:
Almost every list of the people who shaped the modern world is a list of inventors. The engineer who designed a bridge is remembered; the crew that has inspected its cables twice a year for forty years is not, and neither is the official who kept the inspection budget from being cut. Historians of technology have begun to argue that this is not merely unfair but analytically wrong — that most of the work which keeps a society running is maintenance, and that treating it as invisible produces bad decisions.

The argument has an uncomfortable edge. Maintenance is unglamorous [sem glamour] precisely because it succeeds: a bridge that does not fall generates no story. A minister who funds inspection is buying an absence, and an absence is impossible to campaign on. The incentive therefore runs steadily in one direction — towards the ribbon-cutting [inauguração] and away from the far cheaper work of keeping what already stands.

There is also a measurement problem. New construction produces a number — kilometres built, units delivered — that fits neatly into a report. Deferred [adiada] maintenance produces a liability [passivo] that appears nowhere until it appears all at once. Several governments now publish estimates of their maintenance backlog [acúmulo pendente] for exactly this reason, and the figures, once assembled, tend to be larger than the capital budgets printed beside them.

None of this is an argument against building. It is an argument that the real choice is not between building and doing nothing, but between building and keeping — and that only one of those two is ever presented as a choice at all.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem economica sobre desenvolvimento
textos.conteudo:
Money sent home by people working abroad is now larger, in most low- and middle-income countries, than foreign aid, and in many of them larger than foreign investment. It is also the most expensive money in the world to move. Sending two hundred dollars across a border costs, on average, something over six per cent of the sum, and on the dearest routes — usually those serving the poorest senders — it costs twice that.

The reason is not technological. Moving a message costs nothing. What costs money is the last step, in which cash must be handed to a person who may hold no bank account, in a town where a single agent holds the only licence. Competition can exist all along the chain and still fail at that final counter [guichê], and it is there that most of the fee is collected.

Regulation adds to the price in a way that is genuinely hard to unwind. Rules written to stop money laundering [lavagem de dinheiro] oblige a firm to identify both sender and recipient, and doing that costs nearly the same for a transfer of two hundred dollars as for one of two million. Banks facing that arithmetic have withdrawn from whole regions rather than carry the risk, which leaves the remaining operator with less competition and a stronger case for its fee.

Every percentage point taken off the cost of these transfers would put more money into households than most aid programmes do, and it would arrive without a project cycle, a consultant or a report. That is the strongest argument for treating the fee as a policy problem rather than a market outcome — and the reason the target has been missed for a decade is that the expensive part sits precisely in the places least able to attract a second operator.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo de divulgacao sobre politica de saude
textos.conteudo:
The medical problem of antibiotic resistance is well understood and widely reported. The economic problem behind it is neither, and it is the one that explains why so few new antibiotics ever reach a pharmacy.

Consider what a company is being asked to develop. A successful new antibiotic would be given to very few patients, because the moment it works doctors will restrict its use in order to delay resistance — the better the drug, the more carefully it is withheld [retido]. It would be taken for a week rather than for life. And it would be priced against generic [genérico] competitors costing a few cents. A medicine for a chronic condition is the opposite on all three counts, which is where the research money has gone.

The result is a pipeline [linha de desenvolvimento] that runs mostly through small firms and university laboratories, several of which have gone bankrupt [à falência] shortly after regulatory approval — an outcome rare enough elsewhere in medicine to be worth pausing on. Approval was the end of their spending and the beginning of a market that turned out not to exist at the volumes they needed.

Proposals to repair this have converged on one idea from several directions: pay for the drug rather than for the doses. Under a subscription [assinatura], a health system pays a fixed annual sum for access to an antibiotic however much or little it uses, which removes the conflict between selling more and prescribing less. Two countries have run versions of the scheme. It is early, and the sums involved are far below what the analyses say would be needed, but the logic has not been seriously contested.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo sobre infraestrutura e seguranca
textos.conteudo:
Almost everything that crosses an ocean as information crosses it inside a cable roughly the diameter of a garden hose [mangueira de jardim], lying on the seabed [leito marinho]. Satellites carry a small fraction. The rest — financial settlements, telephone calls, the contents of every service people assume to be weightless — travels through a few hundred physical objects that an anchor [âncora] can cut.

They are cut regularly, and this is the part that surprises people. Well over a hundred faults [falhas] occur each year, most caused by fishing gear or by ships dragging anchor in bad weather, and a fleet of specialised repair vessels exists to find and mend them. The system is built to tolerate this: traffic reroutes automatically, and a single break in a well-served region is usually invisible to users.

The vulnerability is concentrated rather than general. A country served by a dozen cables can lose one without noticing; a country served by two cannot, and there are islands and coastal states in the second category for which a simultaneous failure means no international connectivity at all until a repair ship arrives, which can take weeks. The chokepoints [pontos de estrangulamento] are just as uneven: a handful of narrow seas carry a share of the world's traffic out of all proportion to their area.

What has changed recently is not the technology but the reading of intent. A cut that would once have been logged as an accident is now examined for a pattern, and the repair fleet — small, ageing and largely commercial — has become a subject of national security discussion in capitals that had never given it a thought. The cables are no more fragile than they were. What has weakened is the assumption that nobody would want to break them.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre trabalho e tecnologia
textos.conteudo:
The dispute over automating a container port is usually reported as a straightforward contest between efficiency and jobs. The people on both sides of it describe something more specific.

Automated terminals do not, on the available evidence, move boxes dramatically faster than well-run conventional ones. What they do is make the rate predictable. A crane that never tires produces the same number of moves at four in the morning as at midday, and predictability is what lets a shipping line promise a schedule and a factory hold less inventory [estoque]. The gain shows up along the chain rather than at the quay [cais], which is one reason the terminal operator paying for the equipment is often not the party that benefits most from it.

The unions [sindicatos] have read this correctly and have rarely argued that automation does not work. Their position has been about who captures a gain that the port creates and the wider economy collects, and about the fact that this trade is one of the few remaining routes to a middle-class wage without a degree. A settlement [acordo] that protects the current workforce while letting the next generation of those jobs disappear ends the strike without addressing that.

Meanwhile the technical case keeps shifting under both parties. Several fully automated terminals have cost far more than projected and have taken years to reach the productivity of the docks they replaced; a few have been partly reversed. The claim that automation is inevitable and therefore not worth negotiating over has, so far, been the weakest position in the debate.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio de divulgacao linguistica
textos.conteudo:
When a language stops being spoken, the loss is usually described as cultural, and it is. But linguists who work with the last speakers of a language tend to describe something more specific, and harder to replace.

Every language encodes a set of distinctions its speakers found worth making. A few are famous — the terms for snow, the kinship [parentesco] systems that name a cousin on the mother's side differently from one on the father's. Most are quieter. A language spoken along a coast may oblige a speaker to say whether an object is uphill or downhill of the listener rather than to the left or the right, which means its speakers track the terrain continuously, in ordinary conversation, without effort. When the language goes, that habit of attention goes with it, and no dictionary preserves a habit.

The mechanics of the loss are rarely dramatic. Languages seldom disappear because they have been banned [proibidas], though that has happened. They disappear because parents make a reasonable calculation about which language will get their child work, and stop passing the other one on. The decisive generation is usually bilingual and entirely aware of what it is doing.

Revival is possible, and it is not a matter of nostalgia. Where communities have brought a language back, the effect most often reported is not that old texts became readable — it is that a group of people acquired something to do together that was theirs. Whether that counts as a linguistic achievement or a social one is a question the linguists mostly decline to settle.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem analitica sobre politica energetica
textos.conteudo:
Solar panels and wind turbines are now the cheapest sources of electricity ever built, measured by the cost of the energy they produce across their lifetimes. In several countries this has coincided with electricity bills that did not fall, and the distance between those two facts has become one of the most misused numbers in public argument.

The cost of generating a unit of power is not the cost of delivering it when it is wanted. A system built on sources that produce according to the weather needs three things the old one did not: enough transmission [transmissão] to move power from where the wind is blowing to where the demand is; enough storage or flexible capacity to cover the hours when neither sun nor wind is available; and a market design that pays for being available rather than only for producing. Each of those is a real cost, and none of them appears in the figure that gets quoted.

This is not an argument that the transition is expensive in the end. Most analyses find the opposite across a couple of decades. It is an argument about sequence. The cheap part arrives first and is highly visible; the expensive part arrives later and is buried in charges most consumers could not identify on a bill. A public told that the new sources are cheap and then shown a rising bill will draw the obvious conclusion, and it will be the wrong one.

The political consequence is already visible. Support for the transition has proved most durable where the connection between infrastructure spending and the bill was explained before the bill arrived, rather than defended afterwards.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de divulgacao cientifica sobre ecologia urbana
textos.conteudo:
Most birds that migrate long distances do so at night, and a great many of them navigate partly by the stars. The arrangement worked for a very long time and then met, in roughly a century and a half, a change it was not built for.

Artificial light disorients migrating birds in two ways. The first is attraction: a bright, steady light pulls them off course and holds them there, and flocks [bandos] have been recorded circling a single illuminated structure until exhaustion [exaustão]. The second is subtler. Skyglow [brilho do céu] — the diffuse dome of light over a city, visible from many kilometres away — does not trap birds, but it washes out the celestial cues [pistas celestes] they use to hold a heading, across a band of sky that widens every year.

The unusual feature of this problem is how cheaply it can be reduced. Switching off the upward-facing lights of tall buildings during the few weeks of peak migration has produced measurable falls in collisions in every city that has tried it, at essentially no cost and with no loss of function at street level. Very few environmental measures have that profile, which is why the programmes spread quickly once one city published its numbers.

What has not spread as quickly is the harder part. Most artificial light at night is not on tall buildings but on streets and car parks, and much of it points at the sky by accident, through fixtures [luminárias] chosen decades ago. Replacing those is a slow municipal expense with no ribbon to cut, and it is where the remaining problem sits.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo sobre financiamento do ensino superior
textos.conteudo:
A university that recruits students from abroad is usually described as exporting education. In accounting terms it is closer to importing a population: the students arrive, rent housing, pay local taxes and, in most systems, subsidise the tuition [mensalidade] of everyone born in the country, because they pay several times the domestic fee.

That cross-subsidy [subsídio cruzado] has become structural, and it is fragile in a way that is easy to miss. It rests on decisions taken in ministries with nothing to do with education — visa rules, the right to work after graduating, the treatment of a spouse [cônjuge] — and those decisions are made for reasons of domestic politics on a timescale of months, while a university plans on a timescale of years. A country can announce a change in the spring and watch its applications fall by a third by the autumn.

Universities that grew on this income have generally built the capacity the income implied: buildings, staff, whole departments whose viability assumed the flow would continue. When it stops, the cuts do not fall on the courses the international students were taking. They fall wherever the deficit [déficit] can be closed fastest, which in practice has meant languages, classics and the smaller sciences — subjects with few students and no obvious outside revenue.

The uncomfortable observation is that the model was working as designed. Nobody hid the dependency; it appeared in every annual report. What was missing was any mechanism that made the exposure costly to ignore while the money was still arriving.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre regulacao e consumo
textos.conteudo:
The economics of repairing a device are settled long before it breaks. If the screws [parafusos] are standard, the battery is held by a clip rather than by glue [cola], the diagnostic software is available and a spare part [peça de reposição] can be bought by anyone, then a repair costs a fraction of a replacement and a used device holds its value. If any one of those conditions fails, the arithmetic reverses, and the same device becomes cheaper to replace than to fix.

Manufacturers have generally argued that closed designs follow from making devices thinner, more water-resistant and safer to handle. There is something to this: glue does seal a seam [juntura], and a badly fitted battery is genuinely dangerous. But the argument has been weakened by the parts of the practice that have nothing to do with engineering — software that refuses to recognise a component because an authorised centre did not install it, and manuals released only under contract.

The regulations now appearing in several markets mostly target that second category. They require that spare parts and manuals be sold to independent shops on the same terms as to authorised ones, and that software not treat a genuine part as counterfeit [falsificada]. What they do not do is mandate a particular design, which is a deliberate choice: writing engineering into law tends to freeze it.

The early effects have been modest and mostly indirect. Repair shops report shorter waits for parts. The larger change is that resale values have begun to reflect repairability, which puts the incentive where it was always going to work best — in the price a buyer is willing to pay.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio sobre linguagem publica
textos.conteudo:
There is a sentence that surfaces whenever an institution has done something indefensible, and it repays reading slowly: 'We regret that some people were offended.' Every word in it is doing work, and none of the work is apology.

An apology has a fixed structure. It names the act, accepts that the actor performed it, and offers something — a change, a restitution [reparação], at minimum a commitment. The sentence above performs none of those operations. It names no act. Its subject is not the institution but the feelings of other people, which relocates the problem into those who noticed it. And 'some' does further work, quietly implying that the reaction was not general.

What makes the formula durable is that it is not a lie. The institution does regret the situation, and people were indeed offended. This is why it survives legal review, which is usually the point: counsel [advogado] will approve any statement that concedes no fact, and a statement that concedes no fact is the one thing an apology cannot be.

The research here is unusually consistent. Apologies that name the act and accept responsibility reduce the likelihood of litigation [litígio] rather than raising it, and several health systems have adopted disclosure [divulgação] policies on that evidence. The obstacle has never been the finding. It is that the person who must sign the apology is rarely the person who bears the cost of not making one.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem economica sobre risco climatico
textos.conteudo:
Insurance works by pooling [reunindo] risks that are independent of one another. A fire in one house and a fire in another are unrelated events, so a company can hold reserves against a predictable number of them. A flood is not like that. It arrives everywhere at once, which is why flood cover has always been the hardest line to write, and why the state is involved in it in almost every country.

What has changed is that the calculation now has to be made forwards rather than backwards. An insurer prices next year using the record of past years, and that method holds only while the past remains a guide. Where it stops being one, the honest response is either a far higher premium [prêmio] or no offer at all — and both of those, arriving in a market where people have already bought their houses, look less like a technical adjustment than like an eviction [despejo] notice with a stamp on it.

The pattern that follows is by now familiar. Private insurers withdraw from the highest-risk areas; a state scheme steps in to cover what the market will not; the state scheme charges below the actuarial price, because charging the true one is politically impossible; and the gap becomes a subsidy that encourages building exactly where the risk is greatest. Every step is reasonable and the sequence is not.

Some jurisdictions have begun trying to break it by tying support to relocation or to physical protection rather than to rebuilding in place. These schemes are early and expensive, and they have the one feature the previous arrangement lacked: they treat the premium as information about where it is wise to live, rather than as a bill to be softened.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo sobre evidencia e politica publica
textos.conteudo:
Adolescent sleep does not run on the same clock as adult sleep. Around puberty the release of melatonin [melatonina] shifts by roughly two hours, so a teenager told to sleep at ten is being asked to sleep at what the body registers as eight. The finding is old, has been replicated in several countries, and is not seriously disputed.

Its policy implication is straightforward, which is what makes the past twenty years interesting. Districts that moved the start of secondary school from around half past seven to after half past eight reported the results the biology predicted: more total sleep, better attendance and — in the studies able to measure it — fewer road accidents among the youngest drivers. Nothing here required a new discovery.

The obstacle was never the evidence. It was the bus. A district running one fleet across three tiers [turnos] of schools saves a great deal by staggering [escalonar] their start times, and secondary schools are usually placed in the earliest tier because their students can be left unsupervised at the other end of the day. Moving them means either buying buses or sending the youngest children out in the dark, and the second option produces the more alarmed parents.

So the reform has advanced where it could be paid for and stalled [empacou] elsewhere, in a pattern that has nothing to do with how convincing anyone found the research. It is a useful example of what a scientific consensus can and cannot accomplish on its own.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo sobre instituicoes e governanca
textos.conteudo:
The most reliable early sign that a government is in trouble is not a fall in a statistic. It is the moment the statistic stops being published.

Official numbers are a strange kind of infrastructure. They cost little, almost nobody notices them, and they underwrite [dão sustentação a] an enormous amount: contracts indexed to inflation, transfers between levels of government, the pension a person receives, a company's decision to build a factory. A statistical office that loses its independence does not announce the fact. Series are discontinued for methodological reasons, publication dates slip, a definition is revised so that comparison with last year becomes impossible.

The damage is slower than a devaluation and harder to reverse. Trust in a number is built across decades of unremarkable publication and destroyed the first time a figure is visibly convenient. And once the official series is doubted, private substitutes appear — supermarket price trackers, satellite estimates of night-time light, employment indices assembled by payroll [folha de pagamento] firms — which is not the reassurance it appears to be. Those substitutes cover what is profitable to measure, and they are not available to the people who most need the number.

What makes the problem tractable is that the safeguards [salvaguardas] are known and dull: a calendar of releases fixed in advance, a legal separation between the office and the ministry, microdata released to researchers who can check the aggregate. None of it is expensive. All of it is far easier to establish in a year when nobody wants to interfere.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem cultural sobre industria da musica
textos.conteudo:
The length of a pop song fell by about a fifth in the decade after streaming became the dominant way people listen, and the intro — the instrumental opening that once ran fifteen or twenty seconds — has all but disappeared. Neither change was decided by anybody. Both follow from a single accounting rule.

A stream counts, and generates payment, once the listener has heard about thirty seconds. Below that threshold [limiar] it is worth nothing at all. Every incentive in the system therefore points at the first half-minute: reach the chorus [refrão] early, put the hook at the front, and leave the listener no quiet stretch in which to skip. A three-minute song with two choruses earns more than a five-minute song with one, because it is played more often and skipped less.

Musicians describe the constraint without much drama; every era of recorded music has had one, and the three-minute single of the twentieth century was set by the physical capacity of a disc rather than by artistic judgement. What is different now is the speed of the feedback. A producer can see, within days, exactly where listeners stop, and the temptation to edit against that curve is very hard to resist.

The interesting question is what the rule selects against rather than what it rewards. Slow development, a form that only pays off at the end, an album meant to be heard in order — none of these is prohibited, and all of them now cost their maker money to make. That is a different kind of pressure from censorship [censura], and in the long run possibly a more effective one.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio literario breve
textos.conteudo:
A writer who publishes without a name is usually assumed to be hiding from something: a government, an employer, a family. Those cases exist and they are the serious ones. But a great many pseudonyms [pseudônimos] have been adopted by people in no danger whatsoever, and their reasons are worth separating out, because they say something about what a name does to a text.

A name carries a record. Once a reader knows who wrote a sentence, the sentence arrives carrying everything else that person has written, plus their photograph, their nationality and whatever the reader last heard about them. Some of that is useful — it is how a reader decides what to trust. But it also fixes a writer in place. A novelist known for one kind of book who wants to write another discovers that the name has become a genre.

The experiment has been run often enough to be informative. Established writers who published under new names have generally found that the work sold poorly and was reviewed carelessly, and several have described the outcome as clarifying rather than disappointing: they learned how much of the earlier reception had been the name.

None of this argues for anonymity as a rule. A name is also accountability, and a writer who can be found is a writer who can be answered. The point is narrower — that a byline [assinatura] is not a neutral label attached to a finished text. It is part of the text, and it is read first.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre economia do trabalho
textos.conteudo:
Roughly half the world's workers are employed informally: no contract, no registration, no contribution towards a pension they will one day need. Governments tend to describe this as a problem of enforcement, and most formalisation drives have been built on that description — inspections, fines, registration campaigns, the occasional amnesty [anistia].

The results have been poor, and the reason is visible from inside a small business. Registering means paying tax on a margin [margem] that is already thin, complying with rules written for firms fifty times larger, and becoming visible to every official who might want something. Against that, the benefits are real but slow: access to credit, the ability to sell to a large buyer, a pension that pays decades later. An owner weighing an immediate certain cost against a distant probable benefit does what anyone would do.

The programmes that have worked treated the calculation as the thing to be changed rather than the behaviour. Simplified regimes that replace several taxes with a single low payment; registration that takes an hour instead of a month; and — most effective of all — making formality the condition for something the owner already wants, such as selling to a government buyer or accepting the card payments that customers prefer.

None of this reaches the hardest cases: the street vendor [vendedor ambulante] with no premises, the domestic worker in a private home, the very small farm. Those require something different, and the honest position is that no country has solved them. But the middle of the distribution — the shop with four employees — has moved wherever the arithmetic was changed rather than policed.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem cientifica ambiental
textos.conteudo:
The metals used in batteries also lie, in enormous quantity, on the floor of the deep ocean, in lumps [nódulos] the size of a potato that formed over millions of years. Collecting them requires no drilling and no blasting: a machine drives along the seabed and picks them up. On that description the case is easy, and it is the description most often given.

What the description leaves out is the plume [pluma]. The machine disturbs the top layer of sediment, and because there is almost no current down there to disperse it, the cloud travels slowly and settles across a very wide area. The organisms living in that layer are adapted to a place where nothing has changed for a very long time, and the recovery times measured after small experimental tracks [trilhas] are counted in decades. Some tracks cut in the 1980s are still visible and still less populated than the ground beside them.

The regulatory position is genuinely unusual. Mining in international waters cannot begin until an authority made up of member states agrees a code, and that code has been under negotiation for years, with pressure arriving from both directions — companies that have spent heavily on equipment, and states seeking a moratorium [moratória] until the ecology is better understood.

The argument that settles it may not be ecological at all. Battery chemistries have been changing quickly, and more than one of the metals these nodules were valued for is now used in smaller quantities than when the deposits were first surveyed. A resource can lose its case by becoming unnecessary.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo sobre saude global e industria
textos.conteudo:
During the last global health emergency, several countries discovered that the constraint on vaccinating their populations was not money and not regulatory approval. It was that the doses were manufactured in a small number of places, and those places supplied their own governments first. This was not a conspiracy; it is what almost any government would do, and it is precisely why the arrangement was fragile.

The response has been a wave of investment in regional manufacturing, and the early lesson is that the factory is the easy part. A plant can be built in two years. Qualifying it takes longer: regulators must inspect it, buyers must come to trust it, and the staff who run a sterile [estéril] line are trained over a decade rather than a season. Several new facilities stand finished and idle [ociosas] because no order has arrived.

The orders are the real problem. A regional plant competes with established suppliers whose scale makes them cheaper, and no health ministry buying on a limited budget can easily justify paying more for the same product on the argument that it might matter in an emergency which has not happened. Capacity used only in a crisis has to be paid for between crises, and nobody has designed a good way of doing that.

Some governments have begun writing that payment explicitly into their contracts — a guaranteed minimum volume, or a fee for standing ready. It is an unglamorous instrument and it looks like waste on a spreadsheet in every year that nothing goes wrong. Which is, of course, the objection that was raised about strategic stockpiles [estoques estratégicos], right up to the moment they were needed.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre trabalho e plataformas digitais
textos.conteudo:
Every large platform depends on a workforce its users never see and which it rarely names in its own reports. Content moderators [moderadores] review the material that automated systems flag or miss, and the work is almost always contracted out to firms in countries where wages are lower, on terms that keep the relationship at arm's length.

The task is harder than the job title suggests. A moderator applies a rulebook [manual de regras] of several hundred pages to material that is often ambiguous, in languages and dialects the rulebook was not written for, against a time target measured in seconds per item. Accuracy is audited against the rulebook rather than against any outcome, so a moderator who correctly judges a post to be dangerous but files it under the wrong heading is marked wrong.

The psychological cost is documented and has been the subject of litigation in several countries. What gets discussed less is the structural consequence: high turnover [rotatividade] means the people applying the rules are usually new to them, and the accumulated judgement of someone who has done the work for years — the thing that would most improve the decisions — is exactly what the arrangement fails to retain.

Automation is offered as the answer, and it has genuinely absorbed the easiest categories. But the residue [resíduo] left to people is, by construction, the ambiguous part: satire, a reclaimed insult, a threat phrased as a joke, a photograph whose meaning depends on where it was taken. That residue does not shrink at the same rate as the volume, and it is the part where being new to the rulebook costs the most.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio sobre literatura e traducao
textos.conteudo:
A translator is often described as someone who carries a text across a border without dropping anything. The image is comforting and wrong, and translators are usually the first to say so.

Consider a single problem. English has one word for the second person, while Portuguese, French and dozens of other languages have two: one for intimacy or condescension [condescendência], one for distance or respect. A novel in which two characters move from the formal form to the familiar one has, at that moment, told the reader something about the relationship without describing it. Translated into English, the moment simply vanishes — there is no wrong choice available, because there is no choice at all. A good translator will usually rebuild the effect somewhere else, through a shift in register or a first name suddenly used, which means the English reader receives the information but not in the place the author put it.

This is the ordinary condition of the work, not a failure of it. Every translation is a series of decisions about what to preserve when preserving everything is impossible, and those decisions are interpretive [interpretativas]. Two competent translators produce different books from one original, and neither of them is wrong.

The consequence for a reader is worth stating plainly. A translation is not a window onto a text; it is a performance of it, closer to a recording of a piece of music than to a photograph of a painting. Asking which translation is accurate is usually the wrong question. Asking what each one decided to protect is the useful one.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre politica urbana
textos.conteudo:
The reason a city fails to build enough housing is rarely that it lacks land or money, and almost never that developers [incorporadoras] are unwilling. It is that the decision to permit a building is taken by a body which hears from the people nearest to it and from nobody else.

The asymmetry is structural rather than moral. A new block imposes concentrated, immediate and legible costs on a small number of existing residents: noise for two years, a changed view, more cars on one street. It delivers diffuse, delayed and invisible benefits to people who do not yet live there and therefore cannot attend the meeting. One of those groups is in the room. The other does not exist as a constituency [eleitorado] and never will, because by the time its members arrive the decision has been taken.

This explains a pattern that otherwise looks like hypocrisy. The same city can hold a large majority in favour of building more housing in the abstract and reject nearly every specific proposal, without a single person changing their mind. The general question is answered by everyone; the particular one is answered only by the neighbours.

The reforms that have worked accept the asymmetry instead of scolding [repreender] it. Setting the rules at a level where the affected group is larger — a whole city or region rather than one street — restores part of the balance, as does letting anything that meets a published standard proceed without a discretionary [discricionária] hearing. Both approaches move the decision away from the meeting, which is the one place the missing side can never appear.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de divulgacao sobre pesquisa clinica
textos.conteudo:
The placebo effect is usually explained as a form of deception: a patient believes they are receiving treatment, and their symptoms improve because of the belief. That account is now known to be incomplete, and the evidence against it comes from an experiment that sounds like a joke.

In an open-label placebo trial, patients are told explicitly that the pill contains no active ingredient. They are told why the researchers think it might help anyway, and they are asked to take it on schedule. Several such trials — in chronic pain, in irritable bowel syndrome, in fatigue [fadiga] — have reported improvements over patients given no pill at all. Nobody was deceived, and something still happened.

What that something is remains genuinely open. The leading explanations involve the ritual rather than the belief: the act of taking something at a fixed hour, the attention of a clinician, the expectation built into a routine. These are not nothing. They are also not specific to any illness, which is why the effect shows up mostly in conditions measured by what the patient reports rather than by what an instrument records. A placebo does not shrink a tumour [tumor].

The practical implication is narrower than the headlines suggest, and more interesting. It is not that pills can be replaced by rituals. It is that the ritual is already part of every treatment, is currently unmeasured, and is delivered inconsistently — a ten-minute consultation and a two-minute one contain different amounts of it, and no trial has ever been designed to find out how much.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo de politica economica internacional
textos.conteudo:
For thirty years the standard advice to governments was that picking industries was a mistake: officials could not know which technologies would matter, and the attempt would end in expensive factories making things nobody wanted. That advice has been abandoned almost everywhere, and it is worth being precise about why, because the reasons are not the ones usually given.

The first is that the original argument was never as strong as it sounded. The countries held up as models of leaving matters to the market had in fact spent enormous sums on defence research, on agricultural research and on the infrastructure that carried the results to industry — industrial policy under another name, and none of it counted as such.

The second is that the objective changed. Choosing an industry because it will be profitable is a bet, and the criticism of that was fair. Choosing one because a country cannot afford to be unable to make it — medicines, transformers [transformadores], certain chips — is a different kind of decision, closer to insurance, and it is judged by a different standard. An insurance policy that never pays out is not a failed investment.

The risk has moved rather than disappeared. When several large economies subsidise the same industry at the same time, the result is capacity far beyond what anyone needs, prices that fall below cost, and a set of governments each unable to be the first to stop. That outcome does not require any official to have chosen the wrong industry. It only requires that they all chose the right one.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre recursos hidricos
textos.conteudo:
An aquifer [aquífero] is the only major resource that most countries allow anyone standing above it to take without measurement. A farmer drills a well [poço], installs a pump [bomba] and extracts as much as the pump will lift. The volume is not recorded, the total taken by all the wells together is not known, and the level falls.

The physics is unforgiving in a specific way. Surface water announces a shortage: the river is visibly lower, and everyone sees it at the same moment. Groundwater does not. The first sign for an individual user is that the pump no longer reaches, which is solved by drilling deeper — an option available to whoever can afford it and to nobody else. The shortage therefore arrives as inequality before it arrives as scarcity, and the people who feel it first have the least capacity to raise it.

Where extraction has been brought under control, the mechanism has almost never been a ban. It has been measurement followed by a shared allocation [alocação]: meters on the wells, a published total that the basin [bacia] can sustain, and a right to a share of it that a user may sell to another. Selling matters more than it appears — it turns the water an efficient farmer does not use into money, which is a far stronger incentive than an inspection.

What none of these schemes has managed is the initial allocation. Deciding who gets what share of a resource everybody has been taking freely is a distributional question, and dressing it up as a technical one has been the surest way to lose the years in which the aquifer could still have been saved.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio critico sobre indicadores
textos.conteudo:
A ranking is a claim disguised as a measurement. It selects a handful of things that can be counted, assigns each a weight that somebody chose, adds them up and produces an order that looks like a fact. The weights are the argument, and they are almost never the part that gets discussed.

University rankings are the clearest case, because their effects are so easy to trace. A table that gives weight to the ratio of staff to students will, within a few years, find universities hiring staff they do not need for teaching. One that counts citations will find departments reorganised around the fields that cite most heavily, which are not the fields that matter most. None of this involves cheating. Each institution is doing precisely what the published method rewards.

The deeper trouble is that a ranking has to be stable enough to be worth reading and volatile [volátil] enough to be worth reading again. That requirement is met by adjusting the method, which means a change in position may reflect a change in the institution, a change in the formula, or neither. Readers are not told which, and the compilers frequently cannot say.

What survives all of this criticism is the demand. A family choosing between two places, a minister allocating money, a student in another country with no way to visit — each of them needs an ordering, and 'it depends on what you value' is a true answer that helps nobody. The rankings persist because the alternative on offer has been nothing at all.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre energia e clima
textos.conteudo:
Cooling is the only major energy demand that rises with the very thing it protects people from. A hotter year sells more air conditioners, each of which raises electricity demand at exactly the hours when a grid is already strained [tensionada] and — because most of them leak refrigerant [fluido refrigerante] across their working lives — adds to the warming that produced the demand. It is the clearest feedback loop in the whole energy system.

The equity dimension is unusually stark. Air conditioning is the difference between a heatwave that is unpleasant and one that kills, and mortality during extreme heat falls sharply in cities where it is common. It is also expensive to buy and expensive to run, which puts it out of reach exactly where the heat is worst and the grids least reliable. Calling it a luxury has become harder to defend as temperatures have risen.

The technical picture is more encouraging than the political one. The efficiency of the units on sale varies by a factor of three at similar prices, which means the same cooling could be delivered for a fraction of the electricity if the worst models simply left the market. Minimum standards achieve that, cost the consumer nothing across the life of a unit, and have been adopted slowly, because the saving accrues [se acumula] to the buyer over years while the higher price is paid at the counter.

The largest gains, though, are not in the machine. A building designed with shade, ventilation and reflective surfaces needs a smaller unit running fewer hours, and none of that shows up in an energy statistic as cooling at all. It shows up as cooling that was never required.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de divulgacao sobre metodo cientifico
textos.conteudo:
Few fields produce as many confident and contradictory headlines as nutrition, and the reason is not that the researchers are careless. It is that the question is close to impossible to ask cleanly.

To establish that a food causes an outcome, you would randomly assign thousands of people to eat it or not eat it, for thirty years, without their knowing and without anything else in their lives differing. None of that is achievable. So the field relies on observation: large groups are asked what they eat, usually by questionnaire, and are followed for years. People misremember, and they misreport in a patterned way — under-recording whatever they believe to be unhealthy — so the error is not random noise that averages out.

Then there is confounding [confundimento]. People who eat more vegetables also exercise more, smoke less, sleep more and earn more. Statistical adjustment can remove part of that, but only the part that was measured, and the untidy remainder is exactly where the effect being claimed would sit. This is why a finding can survive twenty observational studies and still fail the first trial that tests it directly.

What follows is not that nothing is known. The largest effects — that severe deficiencies cause disease, that heavy consumption of alcohol and of processed meat raises specific risks — have been established repeatedly and by several methods. The uncertainty lives in the small effects, and it is the small effects that make headlines, because the large ones stopped being news decades ago.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo de economia politica internacional
textos.conteudo:
Announcements that the dollar is about to lose its central role arrive on a reliable schedule, and so do the rebuttals [refutações]. Both tend to argue about the wrong quantity.

Reserves are the figure usually cited, and the dollar's share of them has indeed drifted downwards over two decades. But reserves are the least important of the currency's functions. What matters far more is that most cross-border invoices [faturas] are written in dollars, most commodity contracts are priced in them and most international borrowing is denominated in them — and each of those is held in place by everybody else's choice. A firm invoices in dollars because its competitors do and its own costs are quoted that way; no individual decision to switch pays off unless a great many others switch at the same moment.

That structure makes the arrangement extremely stable and, in a specific way, brittle [quebradiço]. Nothing erodes it gradually. What changes it would be a shock large enough to make the coordinated switch worth attempting — and the most plausible candidate is not a rival currency but the perception that access to the dollar system has become a political instrument rather than a utility.

This is the calculation behind the alternatives now being assembled: bilateral settlement in local currencies, regional payment links, arrangements slower and dearer than the system they duplicate. They are not competitive today, and their sponsors know it. They are being built as insurance, which is a different test — an insurance policy is not judged by whether it costs less than not having one.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre tecnologia e direitos
textos.conteudo:
A facial recognition system is usually described by a single number: how often it is right. That number is close to meaningless on its own, and the reason is worth understanding, because it recurs wherever a rare event is being searched for.

Suppose a system is ninety-nine per cent accurate and is used to scan a crowd of ten thousand people for one wanted individual. It will probably find them. It will also flag [sinalizar] around one hundred people who are not them, because one per cent of ten thousand is one hundred. The system performed as advertised. The list handed to an officer is still ninety-nine per cent wrong, and every name on it is a person who will be stopped.

Accuracy also varies across the people being matched, and by more than the headline figure suggests. Independent testing has repeatedly found higher false-match rates for women, for darker-skinned subjects and for the very young and the very old — differences that reflect the composition of the data the systems were trained on rather than anything about faces. A system reported as one overall number therefore distributes its errors unevenly, and the people it errs about most are frequently those least able to contest a stop.

None of this is an argument that the technology never works. It is an argument that the deployment matters more than the algorithm. The same system that is defensible when it unlocks a phone — one face, one comparison, an instant retry — becomes something else when it is searching a crowd for somebody who is probably not there.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio sobre patrimonio e museus
textos.conteudo:
The argument about objects held in museums far from where they were made is usually presented as a choice between two absolutes: return everything, or keep everything on the ground that a collection is a common inheritance [herança]. Almost nobody working in the field holds either position, and the interesting disagreements lie further in.

Start with what is not in dispute. A significant portion of these collections was assembled during periods when consent was not available in any meaningful sense, and the documentation from those years frequently records the taking without embarrassment, because nobody expected to be asked. Where a specific object can be traced to a specific act, the case for return is not usually contested by curators [curadores].

The difficulty is the rest — objects whose route into a collection is undocumented, or was a purchase from someone who may or may not have been entitled to sell, or a gift given under conditions nobody can now reconstruct. Applying a strict rule to that material either returns things that were legitimately acquired or keeps things that were not, and no version of the rule avoids both errors.

What has moved the discussion is a change of question. Instead of asking who owns an object, several institutions have begun asking who should decide what happens to it — a question that admits of shared answers: joint custody, long loans in either direction, digital access, a veto over how something is displayed. Ownership is binary and produces winners. Authority over a decision can be divided, and almost every agreement reached in the last few years has been of that kind.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre demografia e trabalho
textos.conteudo:
Every projection of an ageing population is presented as a problem of pensions, and pensions are the part most easily fixed: a country can change a retirement age, adjust a formula, and the arithmetic closes. The part that does not close is care.

Care is labour, and it is labour that resists the thing which has raised living standards everywhere else. A factory worker today produces many times what one produced a century ago; a person helping somebody dress produces almost exactly what they did then. That gap is why the cost of care rises faster than everything else even when nothing about it gets worse, and why a country can grow richer and find care less affordable at the same time.

The workforce arithmetic is harsher than the money. The number of people needing help is rising while the number of working-age people is falling, and care work pays badly, is physically demanding and carries little status — a combination that does not attract entrants at any wage a public budget is likely to pay. Most systems have closed the gap with migration, which works and is politically fragile, and with unpaid family labour, which is invisible in every statistic and is overwhelmingly performed by women who leave paid work to do it.

That last point is where the accounting misleads. A country that relies on family care records low public spending on care and treats the figure as an achievement. What it has actually done is move the cost from a budget line to a group of households, where it reappears as forgone [não auferidos] earnings, interrupted careers and, twenty years later, a second generation of smaller pensions.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de divulgacao cientifica sobre cognicao animal
textos.conteudo:
An octopus is the strongest available evidence that intelligence is not one thing. It solves problems, opens containers, recognises individual keepers [tratadores] and behaves in ways any observer would call deliberate — and it does all of this having taken an evolutionary route that separated from ours more than five hundred million years ago, before anything resembling a brain existed in either lineage.

The architecture is not a variation on ours. Most of an octopus's neurons sit not in its central brain but distributed through its arms, and an arm separated from the animal goes on performing coordinated actions, reaching and grasping [agarrando] appropriately. Whether the animal 'knows' what each arm is doing in the way a person knows where their hand is remains unresolved, and the experiments that would settle it are hard to design without assuming the answer.

What sharpens the case is the life history. Octopuses are mostly solitary, live two years or less, and die shortly after reproducing without ever meeting their offspring [prole]. Almost every account of how intelligence evolves in vertebrates leans on long life, social groups and learning from others. The octopus has none of these and is intelligent anyway, which means either that the standard account is incomplete or that intelligence has arisen twice by different routes.

Researchers in the field are notably careful about the word itself. Their working position is that the animal is doing something demanding, that the demand is not the same as ours, and that describing it in our vocabulary is the main obstacle to understanding it.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de artigo sobre financiamento climatico
textos.conteudo:
Climate finance is discussed as one subject and behaves as two. Money for cutting emissions and money for surviving what is already coming answer to different logics, and treating them as one has cost the second dearly.

Cutting emissions produces an asset. A wind farm sells electricity, a factory upgrade lowers a bill, and a lender can be repaid out of the revenue. That is why the great majority of climate finance has gone there: it is investable [investível], and the institutions that move money at scale are built to lend against a return.

Adaptation mostly does not produce one. A sea wall, a drainage [drenagem] system, a warning network, a hospital moved uphill — these avoid a loss rather than generate an income, and avoided losses appear on nobody's balance sheet. The benefit is real, frequently larger per unit spent than the mitigation alternative, and structurally invisible to the instruments that exist. The result is that the countries with the least capacity to borrow are asked to borrow for the thing that will not repay the loan, and are then described as having weak project pipelines [carteiras de projetos].

There have been attempts to build instruments that fit: parametric insurance that pays on a measured trigger [gatilho] rather than an assessed claim, debt clauses that suspend repayment after a disaster, grant windows for the poorest. None of these is large yet. What they share is an acknowledgement that the problem was never a shortage of good adaptation projects. It was that the money available had been shaped, entirely reasonably, for a different kind of project.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre midia e audiencia
textos.conteudo:
The most consequential change in how people consume news is not which outlet [veículo] they trust. It is that a growing share of them are deliberately avoiding it, and the surveys that track this find the same reason given everywhere: not that the news is false, but that it is relentless [implacável] and that reading it changes nothing the reader can act on.

This is a different problem from misinformation and has almost the opposite shape. A person who believes something false can, in principle, be shown evidence. A person who has concluded that following events makes them feel worse without making them more capable has made a judgement about the value of the activity, and is largely right about their own case. Telling them the reporting is accurate does not address what they said.

The industry's own incentives have made it worse. Attention is measured continuously and rewarded immediately, and the material that performs best under that measurement is the material that produces an urgent feeling. An outlet that resisted would lose audience to one that did not, so the equilibrium is not chosen by anybody in particular.

The few experiments that have worked share an unglamorous feature. They tell the reader what happened, what is likely to follow, and what — if anything — is being decided and by whom, which turns a stream of events into something with a shape. Whether that can be sustained at the scale of a daily operation is unproven. What is clear is that the audience being lost is not leaving because it disbelieves the news.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de ensaio de critica literaria
textos.conteudo:
A classic is often defined as a book that has lasted, which explains nothing: the question is why some books last while others, admired at the time by the same readers, do not. The answers usually offered — quality, universality — describe the outcome and then call it the cause.

A more useful account starts from the fact that survival is not passive. A book stays in circulation because institutions keep circulating it: it is taught, it is set for examinations, it is reprinted because a syllabus [programa de curso] guarantees a number of sales, it is translated because a publisher believes a reputation already exists. Each of those decisions is taken by somebody with reasons, and the reasons change. A novel can leave the canon for thirty years and return when a new set of readers finds a question in it that the previous set was not asking.

This does not make the value arbitrary. A book that repays repeated reading is genuinely different from one that does not, and no amount of institutional support keeps a thin text alive once people actually open it. But the durable works are the ones that turned out to be about more than their authors could have intended, and 'turned out' is doing the work in that sentence. It names a process that happens in readers, across generations, and not in the book.

Which is why the most reliable sign that a work has become a classic is not agreement about its meaning. It is sustained disagreement — the kind that keeps producing new readings instead of settling into one.

textos.fonte: Texto original em genero de reportagem sobre transicao energetica
textos.conteudo:
The debate about electric vehicles is conducted almost entirely in terms of cars, and across much of the world the vehicle that matters is a motorcycle. Two- and three-wheelers carry a large share of all passenger trips in South and Southeast Asia and in much of Africa, and they are the vehicles most often used to earn a living rather than to commute [deslocar-se para o trabalho].

For this fleet the arithmetic works differently and works sooner. A motorcycle battery is small, so the cost of electrifying is a fraction of a car's; the daily distance is short and predictable, so range is rarely the binding constraint; and the rider is typically buying fuel every day in cash, which makes the saving immediate and legible in a way it is not for somebody who fills a tank once a fortnight. The obstacle is the purchase price, not the running cost — a rider who would save money within a year often cannot find the money for the first month.

That is a financing problem, and it has been solved in several places by separating the battery from the vehicle. The rider buys the machine without a battery, which cuts the price sharply, and swaps [troca] a depleted [descarregada] battery for a charged one at a station, paying per swap.
